title: Bigger Boxes: Estimate, Then Multiply
goal: I can estimate first, then use an area model for bigger numbers like 247 × 6 and 23 × 14.

card.desc: Bailey grows the area model: three boxes for 3-digit × 1-digit (247 × 6) and four boxes for 2-digit × 2-digit (23 × 14). She makes an estimate first so she can tell if her answer is reasonable.

win: You estimated, built every box, and checked your answer. Meticulous work!

teacher.objective: Bailey estimates a product first (round down and up to whole hundreds or tens), then uses a three-box area model for 3-digit × 1-digit and a four-box area model for 2-digit × 2-digit (23 × 14 = 200 + 30 + 80 + 12). She uses the estimate to judge whether her answer is reasonable.
materials: The Class Lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Grid paper (1 cm squares), scissors and 2 colored pencils
Base-ten blocks if you have them (hundreds flats, tens rods, ones); otherwise quick sketches
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Her Lesson 6 score from last night (Formspree)
Packet (2 pages): page 1 is due Thursday, page 2 is on Thursday's task list

plan.do: Class slide 1. Ask how last night's Show What You Know went and which question was hardest.
Class slide 2. She uses crafty or fearsome about a real character and proves it with an event. Link prompt 3 (a good guess) to estimating.
Class slide 3. Flip all 7 cards; she acts out fearsome and crafty and makes a sentence with approximately.
Class slide 4. 93 × 7 on the whiteboard. Use it as a mini re-teach if her Lesson 6 score was under 90.
Class slides 5–6. 1,200 < 247 × 6 < 1,800 on the whiteboard. She says each estimate aloud before answering.
Class slide 7. She draws the 200 / 40 / 7 rectangle with side 6 and fills the partial products.
Class slide 8. She builds 247 six times and sorts flats, rods and ones into 1,200 + 240 + 42.
Class slide 9. Partial products written in a column before tapping; she checks the answer against the estimate.
Class slide 10. 23 by 14 on grid paper, cut into 4 pieces, count each piece by multiplying (200, 30, 80, 12).
Class slide 11. She points to the matching paper piece as each box is revealed.
Class slides 12–13. She says column × row for each sort card and counts four partial products before adding.
Class slide 14. She teaches you 26 × 13: estimate, four boxes, total 338.
Class slides 15–16. Quick and out loud; she explains the wrong choices.
Class slide 17 on her own: estimate and solve 184 × 6. No hints.
Class slide 18. She says the four steps. Open the course page and sort tonight's items from Wednesday's items.

watch: Doing only two of the four boxes (tens × tens and ones × ones: 16 × 24 = 200 + 24). Have her count boxes before adding; the grid-paper cutout makes the missing pieces visible.
Hundreds with too few zeros (300 × 7 = 210). Say it in words: 3 hundreds × 7 = 21 hundreds.
Picking the most complicated route and losing track. Keep the boxes labeled; she writes each partial product inside its box before adding.
Skipping the estimate. Do not let her start multiplying until the between-numbers are written down.
Losing a regroup when adding three or four partial products. Have her add them in a column, lined up by place.

packet_key.answer: Estimate between 300 and 800 (30 × 10 and 40 × 20; accept 10 × 30 and 20 × 40). 300 + 120 + 20 + 8 = 448 fish.
Two complete sentences naming a character, using crafty, fearsome or meticulous correctly, with one event from the book as proof.

teacher.notes: Tonight she does the After-Class Lesson on her own; it ends with Show What You Know (3 different sets for retakes; she needs 90). This is the heavy two-night stretch: Lesson 6 practice and packet plus Lesson 7 practice and packet page 1. Thursday is Prove it. If she scores under 90, start Thursday with 10 minutes of four-box models on grid paper (she counts the four pieces each time) and have her retake the check before the new lesson. If the misses are estimates, practice the round-down/round-up step on 5 problems aloud.

tasks: Tuesday night: do the After-Class Lesson 7. It ends with Show What You Know. Aim for 90.

Wednesday: do the Lesson 6 Packet (pages 1 and 2).
Wednesday: do the Lesson 7 Practice set.

notes.do: She flips all 7 cards and reads them aloud. She acts out fearsome (a fearsome face) and crafty (a sneaky move).

notes.ask: What is the difference between an estimate and the exact answer? Give me a sentence with approximately.

slides.title: Estimate first
slides.text: Before you multiply, estimate. It tells you about how big the answer should be.

slides.tip: One box for each place: hundreds, tens and ones.

notes.do: Click the steps. She draws a rectangle with three boxes (200, 40, 7) and side 6 on grid paper and writes the partial products inside.
notes.say: One box for each place: hundreds, tens and ones. Three digits means three boxes.
notes.ask: How many boxes will 368 × 7 need? Why? Does 1,482 fit our estimate?
notes.listen: Three boxes, one for each place. Yes: 1,482 is between 1,200 and 1,800.

slides.title: Build 247 six times
slides.text: Build 247 with base-ten blocks: 2 hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones. Now make 6 of them.

steps.text: 6 groups of 2 hundreds = 12 hundreds = 1,200.
6 groups of 4 tens = 24 tens = 240.
6 groups of 7 ones = 42.
Push it all together: 1,200 + 240 + 42 = 1,482. Same as the three boxes!

slides.tip: Each box in the area model is one kind of block: hundreds, tens or ones.

notes.do: If you have base-ten blocks, she builds 247 once, then you both build 5 more. She sorts all the flats, rods and cubes into three piles. No blocks? She draws 6 quick sketches (squares for hundreds, sticks for tens, dots for ones).
notes.say: Look: all the hundreds together are the 200 box. All the tens are the 40 box. All the ones are the 7 box.
notes.ask: How many hundreds flats do you have in all? How many tens rods? How many ones?
notes.listen: 12 flats, 24 rods, 42 ones. When she sees 24 rods, ask: how much is 24 tens? (240).

items.q: This is the area model for 368 × 7. What goes in the 300 box?
no: Too many zeros. 300 has two zeros, so 21 gets two zeros.

items.q: The partial products for 368 × 7 are 2,100, 420 and 56. What is 368 × 7?
no: Add the tens again: 2 tens + 5 tens = 7 tens, so 420 + 56 = 476, and 2,100 + 476 = 2,576.
You left out the 56 from the ones box.

items.q: Is 2,576 reasonable for 368 × 7? Finish the estimate: 300 × 7 = 2,100 and 400 × 7 = ____.
items.why: 4 × 7 = 28, so 400 × 7 = 2,800. 2,576 is between 2,100 and 2,800, so it is reasonable.

notes.do: She writes all three partial products on paper in a column, lined up by place, before tapping.
notes.ask: What goes in the 300 box? How many zeros, and why? Now add the column.
notes.listen: 2,100, 420, 56, total 2,576. If she writes 210, say: 3 hundreds × 7 = 21 hundreds. On item 3 she should check 2,576 against 2,100 and 2,800.

slides.title: Cut the rectangle: 23 × 14
slides.text: On grid paper, draw a rectangle 23 squares across and 14 squares down.

steps.text: Draw a line after 20 squares across. Draw a line after 10 squares down.
Cut along the two lines. You get 4 pieces.
Count each piece: 20 × 10, 3 × 10, 20 × 4, 3 × 4.

steps.text: Put the 4 pieces back together. The whole rectangle is 23 × 14.

slides.tip: Four pieces means four partial products. None can be left out.

notes.do: Give her 1-cm grid paper, a pencil and scissors. She draws the 23 by 14 rectangle, marks the 20/3 line and the 10/4 line, cuts it into 4 pieces and counts each piece using multiplication (not one square at a time).
notes.say: Each piece is a box in the area model. If you lose a piece, you lose part of the answer.
notes.ask: How many squares are in the big piece? The skinny piece on the right? The bottom strip? The little corner?
notes.listen: 200, 30, 80 and 12. If she counts squares one by one, stop her: how many rows and how many in each row? Keep the 4 pieces on the table for the next slides.

slides.title: Four boxes for 23 × 14
slides.text: When both numbers have two digits, split both: 23 = 20 + 3 and 14 = 10 + 4.

steps.text: Draw 2 columns (20 and 3) and 2 rows (10 and 4). That makes 4 boxes.

visual.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 324 220" width="100%" style="max-width:344px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">20</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">3</text><text x="36" y="93.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><text x="36" y="182.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">4</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text></svg>

<svg viewBox="0 0 324 220" width="100%" style="max-width:344px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">20</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">3</text><text x="36" y="93.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="82.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#0A1F3D">20 × 10</text><text x="131.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" font-weight="600" fill="#0A1F3D">200</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="82.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#0A1F3D">3 × 10</text><text x="266.0" y="104.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" font-weight="600" fill="#0A1F3D">30</text><text x="36" y="182.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">4</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="171.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#0A1F3D">20 × 4</text><text x="131.0" y="193.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" font-weight="600" fill="#0A1F3D">80</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="171.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#0A1F3D">3 × 4</text><text x="266.0" y="193.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" font-weight="600" fill="#0A1F3D">12</text></svg>

steps.text: Add all four: 200 + 30 + 80 + 12 = 322. It is between 200 and 600, so it is reasonable. ✅

slides.tip: Four boxes means four partial products. Count them before you add so none gets lost.

notes.do: Click the steps. She points to the matching paper piece for each box as you reveal it.
notes.say: Both numbers have two digits, so we split both. Two columns times two rows makes four boxes.
notes.ask: Which paper piece is 3 × 4? Which is 20 × 10? Is 322 between 200 and 600?
notes.listen: The little corner is 3 × 4 = 12; the big piece is 200. Yes, 322 fits the estimate.

slides.title: Which boxes build 36 × 12?
slides.text: 36 = 30 + 6 and 12 = 10 + 2. Tap a card, then tap the right box.

items.hint: 30 is part of 36 and 10 is part of 12.
6 is part of 36 and 10 is part of 12.
30 is part of 36 and 2 is part of 12.
6 is part of 36 and 2 is part of 12.

items.why: That is adding the parts of 36, not a box.
items.hint: Every box is a part times a part.

notes.do: She says 'column times row' for each card before she taps a box.
notes.ask: Is 3 a part of 12? Is 100 a part of 12? Why is 36 not a box?
notes.listen: 12 = 10 + 2, so 3 and 100 are not parts. 36 is adding the parts of 36, not a part times a part. The total is 432.

visual.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 324 220" width="100%" style="max-width:344px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">30</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">2</text><text x="36" y="93.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><text x="36" y="182.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">5</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text></svg>

no: Those are not products. Multiply column times row.

items.q: Berk's training arena has 16 rows of benches with 24 Vikings in each row. How many Vikings?
no: You did only 20 × 10 and 6 × 4. There are four boxes: 200 + 40 + 120 + 24.
You added 16 + 24. Equal rows means multiply.

notes.do: She writes all four partial products on paper, counts them (1, 2, 3, 4) and then adds.
notes.ask: How many partial products should you have? Did you count them?
notes.listen: Four, every time. If she picks 224 for 16 × 24, she did only tens × tens and ones × ones: point to the two boxes she left out.

slides.title: You lead: 26 × 13
slides.text: Tell me the four boxes, then type.

visual.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 324 220" width="100%" style="max-width:344px;display:block;margin:auto" font-family="Fredoka,sans-serif"><text x="131.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">20</text><text x="266.0" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">6</text><text x="36" y="93.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">10</text><rect x="46" y="34" width="170" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="34" width="100" height="104" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="94.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><text x="36" y="182.0" text-anchor="end" font-size="20" fill="#5b6578">3</text><rect x="46" y="138" width="170" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="131.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text><rect x="216" y="138" width="100" height="74" fill="#F7F0FB" stroke="#8E44AD" stroke-width="3"/><text x="266.0" y="183.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#8E44AD">?</text></svg>

items.why: 200 + 60 + 60 + 18 = 338. It is between 200 and 600, so it is reasonable.

notes.do: She leads. She draws the four boxes on the whiteboard, estimates first (20 × 10 = 200 and 30 × 20 = 600), then fills every box.
notes.say: You are the teacher now. Estimate first, then tell me all four boxes.
notes.ask: What is your estimate? What are the four partial products? How many did you count?
notes.listen: 200, 60, 60, 18 = 338. If she has 278 she left out a 60; if she has 218 she did only two boxes.

no: 560 + 42: 6 tens + 4 tens = 10 tens. Regroup to get 602.
Those are the parts of 59. Multiply each one by 6.

notes.ask: What is the shortcut for 7 × 9? Which partial products build 59 × 6?
notes.listen: 5 nines + 2 nines = 45 + 18 = 63. 300 and 54. For 86 × 7, she must regroup: 560 + 42 = 602.

items.q: Hiccup says the sea dragon is approximately 400 feet long. What does approximately tell you?
choices: The real length is close to 400 feet, but maybe not exactly 400.
The length is more than 400 feet for sure.
Nobody has any idea how long it is.
items.why: Approximately means close to, but maybe not exactly.
no: Approximately means close to, not exact.
It could be a bit more or a bit less.
Approximately means we have a close idea.

choices: count all four boxes and check each fact
skip the estimate to save time
add the two biggest boxes and stop
items.why: Meticulous means very careful about every small detail.
no: Skipping steps is the opposite of meticulous.
A meticulous student would not leave boxes out.
Meticulous means careful with every detail.

items.q: Which word fits? The sea dragon was so ______ that the whole tribe hid behind their shields.
items.why: People hide from something fearsome: frightening to face.
no: Crafty means sneaky-clever. The clue is that everyone hid in fear.
Reasonable means it makes sense. That does not explain hiding.

notes.do: She reads every choice and says why each wrong one is wrong.
notes.ask: Why can a triangle not have 'approximately' 3 sides? What would a meticulous student do on 23 × 14?
notes.listen: A triangle has exactly 3 sides. Meticulous = counts all four boxes and checks each fact.

slides.title: Check for understanding
slides.text: On your own. No help this time.

notes.do: She works alone on paper. You watch, but you do not help.
notes.say: Show me what you can do by yourself.
notes.listen: 1,200 and 1,104 with no help means she is ready for tonight. If she writes 1,080, she lost the ones box; if 672, she lost the zero in 80 × 6 (600 + 48 + 24). Fix it together before she leaves.

slides.title: What you can do now
slides.text: Big numbers are not scary. They just have more boxes.

steps.text: 1. Estimate: round down and up to find the two numbers the answer must be between.
2. Boxes: three boxes for 3-digit × 1-digit. Four boxes for 2-digit × 2-digit.
3. Add every partial product. Count them first so none gets lost.
4. Check: is your answer between your two estimate numbers? Then it is reasonable.

slides.tip: Tonight and Wednesday are busy. Look at your task list and do one item at a time.

notes.do: Click the steps, then open the course page together and read the task list. Show her which items are for tonight and which are for Wednesday.
notes.say: Tonight: the After-Class Lesson and the Lesson 6 practice. Wednesday: the Lesson 6 packet, the Lesson 7 practice and page 1 of the Lesson 7 packet. Read every night.
notes.ask: Say the four steps without looking.
notes.listen: Estimate, boxes, add, check. If she leaves out the estimate, remind her: the estimate catches mistakes.
